justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 139.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 141.5 at one month. This trajectory was driven by the assumption that the underlying asset or indicator is in a relatively stable trend environment, likely with mild positive momentum. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is anchored heavily by recent price action or observed values, leaving little room for large moves. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, mean-reversion tendencies and broader fundamental factors begin to assert more influence, though I still weighted the near-term trend slightly in the bullish direction to arrive at those point estimates.

The width of the confidence intervals expands substantially with time, reflecting the well-understood principle that uncertainty compounds over longer horizons. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, which captures typical intraday or overnight volatility. By one week, that range widens to about 11.4 units as day-to-day noise accumulates. At one month, the interval stretches to 25 units, reflecting the full breadth of economic, technical, and sentiment-driven forces that can materially shift outcomes over several weeks. I also weighted the intervals roughly symmetrically around the point estimate, suggesting no strong skew in either direction at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as unexpected central bank policy announcements, geopolitical escalations, or surprise earnings or data releases that dramatically shift market sentiment. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in risk appetite, liquidity disruption, or a technical breakdown below key support levels could drive the outcome well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a significant positive catalyst — stronger-than-expected economic data, a policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could push values above the upper bound. These tail events are by definition not fully captured within a 90% confidence interval, meaning roughly a 10% probability exists that outcomes land outside the stated range entirely.

Finally, model uncertainty itself is a source of risk worth acknowledging. The forecast relies on assumptions about volatility regimes and trend persistence that may not hold if the underlying environment shifts structurally. If realized volatility turns out to be significantly higher than the historical baseline used to calibrate the intervals, all three confidence intervals would prove too narrow in hindsight. Conversely, in a very low-volatility, range-bound environment, even the one-month interval might prove wider than necessary.
